sections.b: After the wall, Nehemiah stands with Ezra at the reading of the law (Nehemiah 8:9), heads the list of those who seal the covenant (Nehemiah 10:1), repopulates Jerusalem by lot (Nehemiah 11:1–2) and leads one of the two choirs at the wall's dedication (Nehemiah 12:31–40). After twelve years as governor he returns to Artaxerxes and then comes back for a second term (Nehemiah 13:6–7), when he clears Tobiah out of the Temple, restores the Levites' support, shuts the gates on the Sabbath and confronts men who married foreign wives. His memoir ends with the prayer "My God, remember me for good" (Nehemiah 13:31). The Talmud faults him for this self-regard (Bavli Sanhedrin 93b); others read the prayers as a servant's dependence on God.

uncommon: Some scholars think Nehemiah's name in 8:9 and 12:26 was added by an editor, and that he and Ezra never worked together.

sections.b: Ezra appears in Nehemiah only in chapters 8 and 12. He reads the law from a wooden platform to the assembled people from dawn to noon, blesses the LORD, and the people answer "Amen, amen" (Nehemiah 8:1–8). The next day the leaders study with him, and the Feast of Booths is kept with the law read daily. He walks at the head of one choir at the dedication of the wall (Nehemiah 12:36). Most critical scholars think chapter 8 once belonged with Ezra 7–10, and 1 Esdras tells it straight after the marriage reform (1 Esdras 9:37–55). The rabbis traced to this day the practice of reading the Torah in public with a translation (Bavli Megillah 3a).

common: Ezra's public reading of the law in Nehemiah 8 is often called the birth of the synagogue's reading of Scripture.

sections.b: When the leaders study the law on the second day of the seventh month, they find the command to live in booths (Leviticus 23:39–43). They proclaim it through the towns, and the people bring branches of olive, oil tree, myrtle and palm and build booths on their roofs, in their courtyards, in the Temple courts and in the city squares (Nehemiah 8:13–16). The narrator says Israel had not done it this way since the days of Joshua (Nehemiah 8:17), though Booths had been kept at the return (Ezra 3:4): the point may be the whole people living in booths, or the joy, or the daily reading of the law. The eighth day is a closing assembly (Nehemiah 8:18).

sections.h: The law read, explained and pledged (Nehemiah 8–10)
sections.b: Nehemiah 8–10 shows a community learning to live by a written law. The "scroll of Moses' law" is read aloud to men and women (Nehemiah 8:1–3), explained by Levites (Nehemiah 8:7–8), studied by the leaders (Nehemiah 8:13), read during a fast (Nehemiah 9:3), and then turned into a signed pledge with detailed terms (Nehemiah 10:28–39). Many of the terms interpret the law rather than repeat it, as David Clines showed: they extend the Sabbath to buying from foreigners and set up a rota for the altar wood. In Nehemiah 13:1 Deuteronomy 23 is read and applied at once. What this scroll contained is debated; many think it was the Pentateuch much as it now stands.

Nehemiah 8:8 says the Levites read the law "explaining it as they went." The Hebrew meforash may mean "clearly," "section by section," or "with translation." The rabbis took it to mean translation into Aramaic, which many Judeans of the Persian period spoke, and found here the origin of the Targum, the Aramaic rendering read in the synagogue after each verse of Hebrew (Bavli Megillah 3a; Bavli Nedarim 37b). The same official word appears in the Aramaic letter of Ezra 4:18. Nehemiah 13:24 shows the opposite concern: children who could no longer speak Hebrew at all.

uncommon: Some scholars think the Levites in Nehemiah 8:8 were not translating at all but reading the text in clear sections, with comments.

sections.b: The fast of Nehemiah 9 is the longest act of corporate repentance in the Bible. The Israelites separate from foreigners, read the law for a quarter of the day and confess for another (Nehemiah 9:1–3). The Levites' prayer retells the whole story of Israel as a story of rebellion met by God's mercy, and moves from "they" to "we": "we have done what is wicked" (Nehemiah 9:33). It ends in a written pledge (Nehemiah 9:38), so that repentance leads to concrete commitments. With Ezra 9 and Daniel 9 it forms a group of penitential prayers from the Persian period.

Two kinds of prayer fill these chapters. The Levites' prayer in Nehemiah 9:5–38 is public and liturgical, built from Scripture and spoken for the whole people; Jews still recite Nehemiah 9:6–11 every morning. Nehemiah's prayers in chapter 13 are short and personal: "My God, remember me for this" (Nehemiah 13:14), "have pity on me as your great loyal love allows" (Nehemiah 13:22), and the last words of the book, "My God, remember me for good" (Nehemiah 13:31). They read like asides to God in a report written for him.

sections.h: The fast of the twenty-fourth day (Nehemiah 9)
sections.b: Two days after the joyful Feast of Booths, the people gather fasting, in sackcloth and with soil on their heads (Nehemiah 9:1). The fast is joined to reading the law and confessing sin, a pattern seen in other fasts of the period (Ezra 8:21; Ezra 10:6; Daniel 9:3). The contrast with chapter 8, where the leaders forbade weeping on a holy day, shows that the community knew a time for each.

sections.h: "Great in loyal love" in Nehemiah 9 and 13
sections.b: The prayer of Nehemiah 9 rests on God's self-description to Moses (Exodus 34:6): he is "a God of forgiveness, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and great in loyal love" (Nehemiah 9:17). It praises him as the God "who keeps the covenant and loyal love" (Nehemiah 9:32), echoing Deuteronomy 7:9. Nehemiah uses the same word for his own faithful acts toward the Temple (Nehemiah 13:14) and then asks pity "as your great loyal love allows" (Nehemiah 13:22): his loyalty is set beside God's, and he relies on God's.
sections.refs: Nehemiah 9:17; Nehemiah 9:32; Nehemiah 13:14; Nehemiah 13:22; Exodus 34:6–7; Deuteronomy 7:9

sections.b: The prayer of Nehemiah 9 recalls the calf of cast metal and the words "This is your god, who brought you up from Egypt" (Nehemiah 9:18), using a singular "god" where Exodus 32:4 has a plural. It calls this "great acts of contempt" and yet says that God, because of his compassion, did not desert them in the wilderness (Nehemiah 9:19). The prayer places the calf beside the people's appointing a leader to return to Egypt (Nehemiah 9:17; Numbers 14:4) as the two worst rebellions of the wilderness.

After the confession, the people make a "firm agreement" (amanah) in writing, sealed by their leaders (Nehemiah 9:38). Eighty-four names head it, and all the people, with their wives and children, take on "a curse and an oath" to walk by God's law (Nehemiah 10:28–29). The terms cover marriage, the Sabbath, the seventh year and the support of the Temple, and the pledge ends "We will not desert our God's house" (Nehemiah 10:39). Chapter 13 shows each term broken and enforced again. It is the last of the Bible's great covenant renewals, after those of Moses, Joshua, Josiah and Ezra.
sections.refs: Nehemiah 9:38; Nehemiah 10:1–39; Nehemiah 13:10–31; Joshua 24:25–27; 2 Kings 23:1–3; Ezra 10:3

sections.b: The covenant of Nehemiah 10:31 extends the Sabbath to trade: the peoples of the land may bring goods to sell, but the community will buy nothing on a Sabbath or holy day. When Nehemiah returns, he finds Judeans treading winepresses and carrying loads into Jerusalem, and Tyrian traders selling fish (Nehemiah 13:15–16). He reminds the nobles that Sabbath-breaking brought the city's fall, as Jeremiah had warned (Jeremiah 17:19–27), shuts the gates from dusk before the Sabbath, threatens the traders camping outside, and sets Levites to guard the gates (Nehemiah 13:17–22).

Nehemiah 10:37–39 promises the tithe of the ground to the Levites, with a priest present at collection and a tenth of the tithe carried to the Temple storerooms (Numbers 18:26). At the dedication, men are appointed over the storerooms, and all Israel gives the singers' and gatekeepers' shares (Nehemiah 12:44–47). By Nehemiah's return the Levites have gone back to their fields for lack of support, and one storeroom has become Tobiah's lodging (Nehemiah 13:4–10). Nehemiah restores the tithes and appoints four trustworthy treasurers (Nehemiah 13:12–13). Malachi's complaint about robbing God in tithes probably comes from the same years (Malachi 3:8–10).

sections.h: The seventh year in the covenant (Nehemiah 10:31)
sections.b: The pledge of Nehemiah 10:31 joins two laws of the seventh year: the land left fallow (Exodus 23:10–11; Leviticus 25:2–7) and loans released (Deuteronomy 15:1–2). Putting them in one sentence, "We will let the seventh year go, and let go of every loan," shows the community reading the laws of Exodus and Deuteronomy together. It follows Nehemiah's call to cancel debts in chapter 5.

sections.h: Lots for wood and for the city (Nehemiah 10–11)
sections.b: Lots settle two practical questions in Nehemiah. The priests, Levites and people cast lots for which family will bring wood for the altar at set times through the year (Nehemiah 10:34), so that the fire Leviticus requires never goes out (Leviticus 6:12–13). And the people cast lots so that one in ten moves into Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:1). In both cases the lot shares a burden fairly and leaves the choice to God (Proverbs 16:33).

sections.h: The holy city filled and dedicated (Nehemiah 11–12)
sections.b: Nehemiah 11 calls Jerusalem "the holy city" (Nehemiah 11:1; Nehemiah 11:18) and fills it with leaders, volunteers and one family in ten chosen by lot. In Nehemiah 12 the priests and Levites purify the people, the gates and the wall (Nehemiah 12:30), and two choirs process along the top of the wall to meet in the Temple. "Jerusalem's gladness could be heard from far off" (Nehemiah 12:43). Nehemiah 13 then guards the city's holiness by closing its gates on the Sabbath, with Levites as guards (Nehemiah 13:19–22).
sections.refs: Nehemiah 11:1–2; Nehemiah 11:18; Nehemiah 12:27–43; Nehemiah 13:19–22; Isaiah 52:1; Psalm 48:12–14

sections.h: The priestly houses in Nehemiah 10 and 12
sections.b: Nehemiah gives three lists of priestly houses: those who came up with Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Nehemiah 12:1–7), their heads in the days of Joiakim (Nehemiah 12:12–21), and the priests who sealed the covenant (Nehemiah 10:2–8). They have about twenty-one or twenty-two names and match each other closely. Many of the names, such as Jedaiah, Joiarib, Harim, Abijah, Bilgah and Maaziah, are among the twenty-four divisions of 1 Chronicles 24:7–18, which suggests that the system of courses was still taking shape in the Persian period.

The singers in Nehemiah are Levites descended from Asaph and Jeduthun (Nehemiah 11:17; Nehemiah 11:22). They live in villages around Jerusalem (Nehemiah 12:28–29), have a royal order guaranteeing their daily share (Nehemiah 11:23), sing in two groups facing each other "as David the man of God had commanded" (Nehemiah 12:24), and lead the music at the wall's dedication with Jezrahiah in charge (Nehemiah 12:42). When their shares stop, they go back to their fields (Nehemiah 13:10).
sections.refs: Nehemiah 11:17; Nehemiah 11:22–23; Nehemiah 12:8–9; Nehemiah 12:24; Nehemiah 12:27–47; Nehemiah 13:10; 1 Chronicles 25:1–31

sections.b: Nehemiah 12:27 names the Levites' instruments, cymbals, lyres and harps, the same trio as in Chronicles (1 Chronicles 15:16), and priests blow trumpets (Nehemiah 12:35; Nehemiah 12:41). The singers are grouped in two choirs that answer each other (Nehemiah 12:8–9; Nehemiah 12:24; Nehemiah 12:31). The scene is one of the fullest pictures of Temple music in the Bible outside Chronicles.

sections.h: Separation and mixed marriages in Nehemiah 9–13
sections.b: Nehemiah 8–13 returns to the questions of Ezra 9–10 several times. The fasting Israelites separate from "everyone of foreign birth" (Nehemiah 9:2), and the covenant forbids giving or taking daughters in marriage with the peoples of the land (Nehemiah 10:30). When Deuteronomy 23:3–5 is read, the people separate "all the mixed crowd" (Nehemiah 13:1–3). Nehemiah then finds men married to women of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab, whose children cannot speak Hebrew (Nehemiah 13:23–24). He curses and beats some and makes them swear, citing Solomon's fall (Nehemiah 13:25–27), but unlike Ezra he does not, as told, send wives away; he drives out only the priest married to Sanballat's daughter (Nehemiah 13:28). Readers have seen in this either the protection of a small, endangered community or a harsh exclusion that other texts, such as Ruth and Isaiah 56, resist.
sections.refs: Nehemiah 9:2; Nehemiah 10:28–30; Nehemiah 13:1–3; Nehemiah 13:23–28; Ezra 10:3; Deuteronomy 23:3–6; Ruth 1:16; Isaiah 56:3–7

common: Nehemiah's reform, like Ezra's, aimed to keep the returned community from losing its faith through marriage with neighboring peoples.
uncommon: Some scholars think Nehemiah 13:23–27 shows a milder policy than Ezra 10 because Nehemiah never tried to dissolve existing marriages.

sections.b: Nehemiah confronts men married to foreign women with Solomon's example: no king among the nations was his equal, he was loved by his God, and God made him king over all Israel, yet "Him too the foreign women led into sin" (Nehemiah 13:26). The argument draws on 1 Kings 11:1–8 and the praise of 1 Kings 3:12–13 and 2 Samuel 12:24–25. It is one of the few places outside Kings and Chronicles where Solomon is remembered, and it remembers him for his fall.

When Deuteronomy 23 is read in Nehemiah 13:1–2, its reason for excluding Moabites and Ammonites is repeated: they did not meet Israel with bread and water, and Balaam was hired to curse them, "But our God turned the curse into a blessing" (Nehemiah 13:2; Deuteronomy 23:4–5). The memory of Balaam thus became part of the case for keeping the community separate.

sections.h: Tobiah in the Temple, Sanballat's son-in-law (Nehemiah 13)
sections.b: During Nehemiah's absence, Eliashib the priest, "close to Tobiah," gave him a large storeroom in the Temple courts (Nehemiah 13:4–5). On his return Nehemiah threw Tobiah's goods out and had the rooms purified (Nehemiah 13:8–9). A grandson of the high priest Eliashib had married Sanballat's daughter, and Nehemiah drove him away (Nehemiah 13:28). The two incidents show how closely Jerusalem's leading families were bound to Nehemiah's opponents by marriage and friendship.

Nehemiah 13:28 tells of a grandson of the high priest married to Sanballat's daughter. Josephus tells a similar story set a century later: Manasseh, brother of the high priest Jaddua, married Nikaso, daughter of a Sanballat sent by Darius III, and for him a temple was built on Mount Gerizim with Alexander's leave (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 11.302–347). The Samaria papyri from Wadi Daliyeh (about 375–335 BC) show that a later governor's family still used the name Sanballat, so Frank Moore Cross proposed a Sanballat II and III; others think Josephus moved Nehemiah's episode to the wrong era. Yitzhak Magen, who excavated Mount Gerizim, dates a first sanctuary there to the mid-400s BC; some scholars place it later.

1 Esdras ends with a Greek telling of the reading of the law in Nehemiah 7:73–8:12, placed straight after the marriage reform of Ezra 10 (1 Esdras 9:37–55). It has no Nehemiah: the title "governor" (tirshata) becomes a man named Attarates (Attharates in Codex Alexandrinus), and Ezra is called "high priest and reader." It ends in mid-sentence, "and they were gathered" (1 Esdras 9:55), so the book may be incomplete. Scholars use it in the debate over whether Nehemiah 8 once followed Ezra 10.

In Nehemiah 8–13 the Masoretic margin corrects mostly names: Nebai for Nobai (Nehemiah 10:19), Jeduthun for Jedithun (Nehemiah 11:17), Unni for Unno (Nehemiah 12:9), Melicu for Malluchi (Nehemiah 12:14), Iddo for Adaia (Nehemiah 12:16), and "heads" for "head" of the singers (Nehemiah 12:46). Several of the written forms agree with the Greek. The site follows the written form in names where it has such support (Nobai, Malluchi), except at Nehemiah 12:16, where the parallel list of Nehemiah 12:4 shows that Iddo's house is meant.

sections.b: The prayer of Nehemiah 9 ends with a bitter picture of Persian rule: the people are slaves in the land given to their ancestors, its harvest goes to the kings God set over them for their sins, and the kings rule their bodies and cattle as they please (Nehemiah 9:36–37). Unlike Ezra's prayer, which thanks God for the kings' kindness (Ezra 9:9), it says nothing good of the empire. Yet chapter 13 shows Nehemiah still serving Artaxerxes, "king of Babylon," returning to court in the king's thirty-second year, 433/432 BC (Nehemiah 13:6).
